questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Select the Law of Thought violated in the statement, " I am Tom's kid sister but he is not my brother".

(ii) Identify the Operation of the mind employed when a child sees an object and calls it a ball. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The **Law of Non-Contradiction**. If I am Tom's sister, Tom is my brother, so the statement says that Tom is and is not my brother at the same time and in the same respect.

**(ii)** **Simple apprehension** (conception), the first operation of the mind: the child grasps the idea of the object and names it "ball", without yet affirming or denying anything about it. (The other operations are judgement and reasoning.)
themes: O Level Logic - laws of thought

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Using the Term "Power mongers", as the Predicate Term, "Politicians" as the Subject Term, construct a Particular Negative Proposition.

(ii) Determine the Distribution of Terms in b (i) above. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A particular negative is an O proposition, "Some S are not P": **"Some politicians are not power mongers."**

**(ii)** In an O proposition the subject is **undistributed** ("some" refers to part of the politicians) and the predicate is **distributed** (a negative proposition excludes the subject from the whole class of power mongers). So: "politicians" undistributed, "power mongers" distributed.
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
O Level Logic - propositions and their types

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Given that the variable "J" stands for the statement "Joan will marry" and the variable "M" stands for the statement "Mary will be happy", translate the following symbolic statements into Ordinary Language: $(\sim J \vee M)$

(ii) Given that J is True and M is False, determine the Truth-Value of the statement in c (i) above. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** $\sim J$ = "Joan will not marry"; $\vee$ = "or". So **$(\sim J \vee M)$ reads: "Either Joan will not marry or Mary will be happy."** (It is equivalent to "If Joan marries, then Mary will be happy".)

**(ii)** J = T, so $\sim J$ = F; M = F. Then $\sim J \vee M$ = F v F = **False**.
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Give the Obverse of the Proposition, "Some women are teachers".

(ii) Clearly write out the Middle Term and Conclusion of the Syllogistic argument below:

"No fruits are bitter things.

All oranges are fruits.

Therefore, No oranges are bitter things" (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** "Some women are teachers" is an I proposition. To obvert it, change its quality (affirmative to negative) and replace the predicate by its contradictory: **"Some women are not non-teachers."**

**(ii)** **Middle term: fruits** (it occurs in both premises and not in the conclusion). **Conclusion: "No oranges are bitter things."** (The form is E A E in the first figure, Celarent, a valid syllogism.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) (i) Transform the Syllogism in d (ii) above into the First Order of Enthymeme.

(ii) Identify the Fallacy most clearly committed in the following Argument: "I can't stop drinking alcohol since my grandmother does so". (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** An enthymeme is a syllogism in which one proposition is left unstated. In the **first order** the **major premise** is suppressed. So the syllogism becomes:

**"All oranges are fruits, therefore no oranges are bitter things."** (the major premise "No fruits are bitter things" is understood but not stated.)

**(ii)** **Appeal to the people (argumentum ad populum, the "others do it" form).** The speaker justifies his own behaviour by the fact that someone else does the same; the grandmother's habit is irrelevant to whether he can or should stop. It is a fallacy of relevance.
